opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that human data works best when the robot body is close enough to the human body that the gap is small. That means a humanoid form, or at least human-like arms and hands on some kind of mobile base.

The reason is pretty simple. When you learn from people, from egocentric video, from wearable capture setups, from teleoperation, what you're really capturing is how a human body interacts with the world. Where the head and eyes are, how the arms reach, how the fingers wrap around an object, how people move their torso to get leverage. The more the robot's embodiment differs from that, the more you have to translate, and every translation step loses information or adds error.

So I'd put it like this. You don't necessarily need a full humanoid with legs for everything. A lot of the value is in the upper body: a head-mounted camera at roughly human eye height, two arms with human-like reach and kinematics, and dexterous hands. If you have that, a lot of what humans do in kitchens and homes and factories maps over fairly naturally. Legs matter for some settings, but for manipulation the arms, the hands, and the viewpoint are where the alignment really pays off.

The hands are the hardest part. Parallel-jaw grippers are great for engineering, but if you want to use the enormous amount of human hand data out there, you eventually want hands that can at least approximate human grasps. That doesn't mean five fingers with twenty-plus degrees of freedom on day one, but the closer you get, the more of that data becomes usable.

The other side of this is that I don't think embodiment matching is the whole story. Part of our research is about learning representations that hold up across embodiments, so the model learns what the task is and what the intent is, not just the exact joint trajectory. But practically, the success of human data and the rise of human-like robot bodies are tied together. One makes the other much more valuable. If humanoids keep getting better and cheaper, all the human video and human demonstration data in the world suddenly becomes a training resource, and I think that's one of the most exciting shifts happening in robotics right now.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot needs at least human-like arms and hands, and later identifies the upper body as the main source of alignment with human data.

r002.rationale: The response mentions legs and a mobile base, but does not propose that the lower body support movement in all directions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that the body matters a lot, and I think it matters more than people sometimes want to admit when they talk about "human data for robots."

The core issue is the embodiment gap. When we collect human data, whether that's egocentric video of people doing chores or motion capture of people manipulating objects, the data is implicitly conditioned on the human body. The way I reach for a cup depends on the fact that I have a shoulder, an elbow, a wrist with a certain range of motion, five fingers, tactile feedback in my fingertips. If I take that data and try to transfer it to a two-finger parallel-jaw gripper on a seven-degree-of-freedom arm, a lot of the information is either unusable or actively misleading. The strategies a human uses just aren't the strategies that gripper should use.

So the robot body that benefits most from human data is one where that gap is small. That points toward humanoids, or at least humanoid-ish upper bodies with dexterous, multi-fingered hands. Not because humanoids are magically better at tasks, but because they make the retargeting problem tractable. If the kinematics roughly line up, you can map human hand poses to robot hand poses, human arm trajectories to robot arm trajectories, and the mapping errors are things the robot can learn to correct with a relatively small amount of its own data.

That said, I want to push back a little on the idea that it has to be a full humanoid. I don't think the legs are the important part for most of what we care about in manipulation. A wheeled base with a human-like torso and good hands gets you most of the benefit for household and warehouse tasks. The hands are really the bottleneck. If the hands are bad, human data is close to useless, because almost everything interesting humans do with their hands involves contact-rich, multi-finger coordination.

The other thing I'd say is that it's not just about kinematic similarity, it's also about sensing. Humans have incredibly rich tactile feedback, and a lot of what we do is driven by that, not by vision. If the robot has a human-shaped hand but no tactile sensing, you're still missing a big piece of why the human data looks the way it does. So I think the "right" body for human data is one that's approximately human in the arms and hands, and that has enough sensing that the robot can actually reproduce the closed-loop behaviors humans rely on, rather than just the open-loop trajectories.

The last point, which I think is underrated: the body also has to be cheap and robust enough that you can deploy a lot of them. Human data gets you a prior, but you still need robot data to close the gap, and that only works if the hardware is something you can run for thousands of hours without it breaking or costing a fortune. So the ideal body is human-like enough to transfer, and boring enough to scale.

r001.rationale: The response says the body should be approximately human in its arms and hands, and specifically proposes humanoids or humanoid-like upper bodies to reduce the transfer gap.

r002.rationale: It suggests a wheeled base but does not say the lower body should support holonomic movement or moving in all directions.

astra-6.text:
I think a human-like body makes a lot of sense if you want to learn from human data. There’s a closer correspondence between what you observe a person doing and what the robot can actually do—especially with the arms and hands.

But I wouldn’t say that means every robot needs to be a full humanoid. A robot with two arms on a mobile base could still learn a lot from human demonstrations. The key is whether its capabilities match the parts of the human behavior you’re trying to transfer. Watching someone pick up an object can tell you what to do, but the robot still has to learn how to execute that with its own body.

r001.rationale: The response says a human-like body, especially arms and hands, can help and mentions a two-arm robot, but it does not identify a human-like upper body as a minimum requirement.

r002.rationale: The response mentions a mobile base but does not specify holonomic movement or the ability to move in all directions.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key is how well the robot’s body matches the human actions you’re trying to learn from. If you want to use human video, having arms and hands that can interact with the world in similar ways makes that transfer easier. But that doesn’t necessarily mean you need a full humanoid. A lot of useful tasks could be done with two arms on a mobile base. The question is which parts of the human body you need to preserve for the data to be useful, and which parts you can simplify.

r001.rationale: The response says similar arms and hands make transfer easier, but does not identify a human-like upper body as a minimum requirement.

r002.rationale: The response mentions a mobile base but does not say it should support holonomic movement or move in all directions.
